lesson.grammar_point: modal verbs would, could and might for polite disagreement

listenings.text: People think a good panel is one where everybody agrees. It isn't. The audience remembers the moment when two speakers disagree. But there is a big difference between a debate and a fight. The best speakers I have seen always do the same thing. Before they disagree, they concede one point. They say something like: that might be true, but. And then they give their argument, with one example. The speakers who interrupt all the time lose the room. The audience stops listening to them, even when they are right.

My first debate in English was in Washington, eight years ago. I was very nervous, because my English was not perfect and the other speaker was a native speaker who talked very fast. At one point, he said that Latin American regulators were not independent. I completely disagreed. So I raised my hand and said, could I add something here? Then I gave one example, with numbers, from a real case in my country. After the panel, three people came to talk to me, and none of them mentioned my accent. They all mentioned the example. That day, I learned that the audience cared more about the example than about the accent.

The final panel of the infrastructure forum in New York turned into a lively debate yesterday. Speakers disagreed on one question: do investors care more about returns or about regulation? A banker argued that high returns were enough to attract foreign money. A fund manager from Canada conceded that high returns could attract investors in the short term, but she said that long-term investors would always look at the rules first. At the end, the moderator asked the audience to vote. Most of the audience voted that stable regulation matters more.
